source: Synthetic cases linked to 8C-2D.1, NOT production questions, real answer keys or learner outputs.

exemplars.title: How far is the 12th marker from the 4th marker?
exemplars.question: The markers are equally spaced 6 m apart on a straight path. Find the distance from marker 4 to marker 12.

steps.learnerExplanation: Put a small mark for the 4th marker and another for the 12th. Each neighbouring pair has a 6 m gap.
The marker numbers tell us the positions, not the number of gaps. Subtract 4 from 12 to count 8 gaps.
All 8 gaps are 6 m long. Multiply 8 by 6 to get the whole distance of 48 m.
Between the 4th and 5th marker there is only one gap, even though two markers are shown. That gap is 6 m.

representation.description: Label the 4th and 12th markers, then show eight identical gaps of 6 m between them.

misconception.incorrectApproach: Count nine markers from the 4th through the 12th, then multiply by 6.
misconception.correction: Mark two neighbouring positions and point to the one gap; intervals equal the difference in position numbers.

comparison.advantageHypothesis: Explicitly counting the gaps prevents an endpoint off-by-one error.

exemplars.title: One gap between two adjacent markers
exemplars.question: The markers are equally spaced 9 m apart. Find the distance from the 1st marker to the 2nd.

steps.learnerExplanation: Mark the 1st and 2nd markers side by side. There is one equal gap of 9 m between them.
Subtract the first position number from the second: 2 minus 1 gives one gap, not two gaps.
One gap is 9 m long, so the total distance is 1 times 9, which is 9 m.
Point to the single space between the two markers. We count spaces, not the number of markers.

representation.description: Draw two labelled marks with one 9 m gap between them.

misconception.incorrectApproach: Multiply 2 markers by 9 m, as if two markers meant two gaps.
misconception.correction: Trace the space separating the two markers; there is exactly one interval.

comparison.advantageHypothesis: A simple adjacent case makes the gap-count idea visible before larger problems.

exemplars.title: Three linked quantities from a total of 66
exemplars.question: Bella has three times as many objects as Alan. Chen has half as many as Bella. Together they have 66. How many does Chen have?

steps.learnerExplanation: Use Alan as the reference. Bella has three Alan-sized amounts; Chen has half of Bella, not half of Alan.
To avoid half-bars, represent Alan with 2 little equal parts, Bella with 6, and Chen with 3. All bars use the same-sized part.
There are 2 plus 6 plus 3, or 11 equal parts altogether. Divide 66 by 11 to find 6 objects in one part.
Chen has 3 equal parts. Multiply 3 by 6 to find that Chen has 18 objects.
Check: Alan has 12, Bella has 36, Chen has 18; Bella is three times Alan, Chen is half Bella, and 12 + 36 + 18 = 66.

representation.description: Aligned bars contain 2, 6 and 3 equally sized sections respectively. The same section size is used for everyone.

misconception.incorrectApproach: Treat half of Bella as half of Alan when adding the quantities.
misconception.correction: Label each relationship first and split all bars into one common small part.

comparison.advantageHypothesis: Common equal parts reveal why half of Bella is not half of Alan.

exemplars.title: One base unit for three comparisons
exemplars.question: Bella has twice as many objects as Alan; Chen has three times as many as Alan. Together they have 72. How many does Chen have?

steps.learnerExplanation: Both comparisons refer to Alan, so Alan is one reference part in our bar model.
Show Alan as 1 equal part, Bella as 2 parts and Chen as 3 parts. All parts have the same value.
Add 1 plus 2 plus 3 to make 6 equal parts. Divide the total of 72 by 6, giving 12 per part.
Chen owns 3 parts, so multiply 3 by 12 and obtain 36 objects for Chen.
Check Alan 12, Bella 24 and Chen 36. Bella is twice Alan, Chen is three times Alan, and 12 + 24 + 36 = 72.

representation.description: Place three bars of 1, 2 and 3 common parts in alignment.

misconception.incorrectApproach: Assume Chen is three times Bella even though both comparisons mention Alan.
misconception.correction: Underline the named reference in each statement; both comparisons refer to Alan.

comparison.advantageHypothesis: One common reference unit keeps two different multipliers from being mixed.

exemplars.title: A ratio changes after two known additions
exemplars.question: The ratio of quantities A:B was 3:2. A increases by 6 and B increases by 24; the new ratio becomes 1:2. Find the original amount of B.

steps.learnerExplanation: Keep A first and B second in both ratios. The original ratio is 3 to 2; both A and B increase by the stated amounts.
Use a before-state unit u: original A = 3u and original B = 2u. Those before-state units are the same size.
After the additions, the quantities become A = 3u + 6 and B = 2u + 24. Neither quantity stays unchanged.
The new ratio 1:2 means B is twice A after the changes: 2(3u + 6) = 2u + 24. This gives u = 3.
Before: A = 9 and B = 6. After: A = 15 and B = 30. Their ratios are 3:2 and 1:2, and both additions are correct.

representation.description: Two rows for before and after, with A and B columns and a separate change row. Do not equate the before and after ratio units.

misconception.incorrectApproach: Use one unit-size for both 3:2 and 1:2, even though both amounts changed.
misconception.correction: Use separate before/after rows and check the differences in actual quantities.

comparison.advantageHypothesis: The before-and-after table makes changed unit sizes and both additions explicit.

exemplars.title: Two different ratio unit sizes
exemplars.question: Quantities A:B start in the ratio 2:3. A increases by 5 and B increases by 16, giving a new ratio 1:2. Find original B.

steps.learnerExplanation: Write A then B in both rows. The before ratio is 2:3, the after ratio is 1:2, and both changes are given.
Let u be one before-ratio unit. Initially A = 2u and B = 3u; we have not assumed an after-ratio unit.
After the changes, A = 2u + 5 and B = 3u + 16. Both quantities have changed from their original values.
Because the new B is twice the new A, 2(2u + 5) = 3u + 16. Solve to obtain u = 6.
Before A = 12 and B = 18. After A = 17 and B = 34. Both stated changes and both ratios are satisfied.

representation.description: Use distinct before and after table rows so the before unit 6 is not mistaken for the after unit 17.

misconception.incorrectApproach: Assume a 6-object unit still applies after the quantities increase.
misconception.correction: Compare actual amounts in both rows: A and B increase by different amounts, and the new ratio unit equals 17.

comparison.advantageHypothesis: A two-state table prevents the old and new ratio scales from being conflated.
